blurb: Code design, logical gates, magic states, FT architecture. Where the field's center of mass moved after 2024.
narrative: Until 2023 this branch was one where theory ran ahead of experiment. [[bluvstein24]] (a logical processor with transversal gates on reconfigurable arrays) inverted that relationship, and the field's center of mass shifted from physical-qubit performance to logical-layer operation. Three fronts now: lowering thresholds via erasure conversion, exploiting movable connectivity for high-rate qLDPC codes, and running actual algorithms on logical qubits. Every structural card neutral atoms hold over superconductors — arbitrary connectivity, identical atoms — is being cashed in here.

blurb: High-rate codes (qLDPC) enabled by movable connectivity.
Non-destructive imaging, mid-circuit measurement with feedforward, erasure detection. A prerequisite for FT and a distinct optics problem.
narrative: Fluorescence imaging heats and loses atoms — so 'watching while you compute' is its own optics problem. Non-destructive imaging and mid-circuit measurement are prerequisites for error correction, and erasure detection (measurement that knows where an error occurred) is a rare case of a 2022 theory proposal ([[wu22]]) reaching experiment within a year. Small in volume (~2% of the corpus), but the bottleneck of two other branches — gates and QEC — gets resolved here.

blurb: Many-body dynamics, topological phases, spin models. The field's original purpose, predating its life as a computer.
narrative: This is the field's headwater — Rydberg interactions implemented many-body Hamiltonians directly before neutral atoms were ever called computers. Quantum scars ([[turner18]]), discovered by accident on a 51-atom array ([[bernien17]]), upended thermalization lore and became a subfield of their own; the 256-atom spin-liquid observation ([[semeghini21]]) showed analog simulators can discover new phases of matter. Still the corpus's largest mass, but the digital side (QEC, gates) has grown faster over the last three years — whether the headwater is yielding to its tributaries is this map's plot line.

blurb: Alkali vs alkaline-earth, nuclear-spin qubits, metastable states, dual species. Treating level structure as a resource for code theory.
narrative: Which atom to use was once a matter of convenience; it became a matter of resources. Weight shifted from the simplicity of alkalis (Rb, Cs) to the rich level structure of alkaline earths (Sr, Yb) for three reasons: long coherence in nuclear-spin qubits, erasure conversion via metastable states, and a metrology interface through clock transitions. The omg architecture — reading level structure as a design resource for error models — is this viewpoint's apex. Tweezer molecules extend the same logic to broaden the kinds of interactions available.

blurb: Polar molecules in tweezers — long-range dipolar interactions.
Tweezer clocks, spin squeezing, entanglement-enhanced metrology. Possibly the hardware's first practical exit.
narrative: The first practical exit for neutral-atom hardware may be clocks, not computation. Tweezer clocks add single-atom control to lattice-clock precision, and spin squeezing with entanglement-enhanced metrology opens the road below the standard quantum limit. Results like half-minute-coherence tweezer clocks ([[young20]]) show this branch selling the same technology as QEC — individual control, non-destructive measurement — as a different product.

blurb: Reading Rydberg blockade as an independent-set constraint. The analog hardware's one commercial exit and its most contested claim.
narrative: When [[pichler18]] pointed out the structural isomorphism between Rydberg blockade and maximum-independent-set constraints, analog hardware acquired a native problem. [[ebadi22]] (289 qubits) then claimed quantum speedup on that problem head-on — the boldest claim in this corpus. The pattern that followed is the field's in miniature: claim in 2022, audit of its benchmark instances in 2023 — and the gap between those dates is where 'advantage' actually lives. This branch remains the platform's commercial exit; whether it is also a scientific one is being decided in the classical branch, not here.

blurb: Tensor-network baselines, complexity arguments, verification methodology. The branch that measures how well the other branches' claims hold up.
narrative: If the field's claims have consistently outrun the tools for checking them, this branch is where the tools catch up. [[andrist23]] showed [[ebadi22]]'s benchmark instances fall to classical solvers in minutes — and the notable part is who says such things now: rebuttals have moved from outside attack to internal self-verification, including from inside hardware vendors. Tensor-network baselines, hardness analyses, and verification protocols keep raising the price of the phrase 'quantum advantage.' On this map the audit is drawn as a supporting lane; read it as the frontier — every claim in the other ten branches is only as good as what survives here.

blurb: Rydberg gate protocols, pulse design, erasure conversion. One fidelity number decides the viability of every layer above.
narrative: A single two-qubit fidelity number decides the viability of every layer above it — QEC and algorithms alike. Rydberg blockade gates went from the 97% range (mid-2010s) past 99.5% in 2023 ([[evered23]]), entering fault-tolerance-threshold territory; much of that jump came from pulse design (time-optimal control) and from the erasure-conversion idea of making errors visible rather than absent. The question now is not few-qubit records but holding that number across arrays of hundreds.

blurb: Atom number, continuous reloading, vacuum and optics engineering. The scale-vs-quality trade-off keeps getting broken.
narrative: Arrays that bragged about 100 atoms (2017) passed 1,000 (2022), reached 6,100 tweezers ([[manetsch24]]), and continuous operation of 3,000 qubits ([[chiu25]]). The folk theorem that scale costs quality has been repeatedly broken; the bottleneck has moved from optical power or vacuum to continuous reloading — replacing lost atoms in real time. This branch's numbers are the denominator of every roadmap: logical qubit counts cannot exceed physical atom counts.

blurb: Coherent transport: moving atoms without losing entanglement.
Cavity and nanophotonic atom–photon entanglement. Routing around the single-chamber limit with modular architecture.
narrative: There is a ceiling on how many atoms one vacuum chamber can hold, and this branch routes around it not with a bigger chamber but with entanglement between chambers. Cavity and nanophotonic interfaces create atom–photon entanglement; fiber links the modules — the same goal as the scale branch (more qubits) by a different strategy. Telecom wavelength conversion and atom–photon entanglement fidelity are the current bottlenecks; the moment modular architecture works, this branch is promoted from supporting cast to architectural axis.

blurb: Compilers, qubit mapping and routing, control stacks, resource estimation. Computer science in service of the hardware.
narrative: The moment hardware demonstrated logical qubits, the bottleneck moved to software — routing that physically moves atoms, zoned-architecture scheduling, and neutral-atom-specific compilation cannot reuse superconducting toolchains. This branch is the mirror image of classical: both are computer science, but classical rebuts the hardware's claims while software serves them. On this map it is structurally undercounted (much of the literature lives in CS categories) — it is larger than it looks.
